Problem 613. Which institution has the role? Approve the town budget
Knowledge context.
Civic institutions divide responsibilities. A problem can be solved by matching an action to a clearly defined function.
Given facts.

Roles are defined as follows: Town Council makes local policy and approves the budget; Public Works Office maintains roads; Local Court decides legal disputes; Election Committee administers elections; School Board sets school policies. A resident asks which institution should approve the town budget. Cross-domain check: a survey team starts work at 12:00 and works for 2 hour(s) without a break.
Rules.
Match the requested action to the stated role. Do not choose an institution merely because it is powerful or familiar. For the cross-domain check, finishing time = starting time + duration.
Task.
Should the request go first to the Town Council or the Health Office? Why? Cross-domain check: at what time does the team finish?
Step-by-step solution.

1. Identify the action: approve the town budget. 2. Find the role whose definition contains that function: Town Council. 3. Health Office has a different stated role, so it is not the first match. Cross-domain check: 12+2=14, so the team finishes at 14:00.
Answer.
The request should go first to the Town Council. Cross-domain answer: 14:00.
Knowledge takeaway.
Institutional reasoning is role matching, not guessing which body is “most important.”
Formal model.
Bipartite relation between actions and authorized institutional roles.

Answer.
The request should go first to the Election Committee. Cross-domain answer: quorum is met.
Knowledge takeaway.
Institutional reasoning is role matching, not guessing which body is “most important.”
Formal model.
Bipartite relation between actions and authorized institutional roles.

C6. Public budgets and priorities
Problem 616. Choosing a public budget package: case 1
Knowledge context.
Public budgets require choices under limited resources. A transparent model separates costs, benefits, and mandatory obligations.
Given facts.

A town has a budget of 16 units. Projects (cost, benefit): park=(4,5); bridge repair=(6,9); library books=(3,4); drainage=(5,8). Cross-domain check: on a field sketch, 1 cm represents 3 km and two checkpoints are 2 cm apart.
Rules.

Choose a subset whose total cost does not exceed the budget. Maximize total benefit. If a mandatory project is stated, every feasible plan must include it. For the cross-domain check, real distance = sketch distance × kilometres per centimetre.
Task.
Which set of projects gives the greatest total benefit while satisfying every constraint? Cross-domain check: what real distance separates the checkpoints?
Step-by-step solution.

1. Budget limit is 16. 2. Evaluate feasible combinations (and keep the mandatory project if any). 3. The best feasible combination has cost 15 and benefit 22: ['park', 'bridge repair', 'drainage']. 4. No higher-benefit feasible combination exists under the stated costs. Cross-domain check: 2×3=6 km.
Answer.
Choose park, bridge repair, drainage; cost 15, benefit 22. Cross-domain answer: 6 km.
Knowledge takeaway.
Optimization means comparing feasible alternatives under an explicit objective, not simply choosing the cheapest item.
Formal model.
0/1 knapsack with optional mandatory-item constraint; maximize benefit subject to total cost ≤ budget.

C7. Collective choice and preferences
Problem 621. Pairwise collective choice: Park versus Library
Knowledge context.
Group preferences can be aggregated in different ways. Pairwise majority asks a specific question about two options at a time.
Given facts.

Three public projects are considered: Park, Library, Sports Hall. Voter groups and rankings: 4 voters rank Park>Library>Sports Hall; 6 voters rank Library>Sports Hall>Park; 2 voters rank Sports Hall>Park>Library. Use pairwise majority: compare two options at a time; each voter supports the one ranked higher.
